content: Safe methods to improve cognitive function in individuals without cognitive impairment are highly desirable, as they could contribute to improved quality of life and professional achievements. L-carnitine has been suggested to enhance cognitive function in certain conditions, but its effectiveness in cognitively healthy individuals remains controversial. To date, no systematic review has been conducted to evaluate its efficacy in this population. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of L-carnitine for cognitive enhancement in individuals without cognitive impairment. A comprehensive search was conducted in the ALOIS database, the Cochrane Dementia and Cognitive Improvement Group's Specialized Register, on November 4, 2016. Search terms included 'L-carnitine,' 'acetyl-L-carnitine,' 'propionyl-L-carnitine,' 'ALC,' 'PLC,' 'ALCAR,' and 'ALPAR.' Additional searches were performed in other databases, and bibliographies of identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were reviewed. Authors, experts in the field, and pharmaceutical companies were also contacted to identify any additional published or unpublished data. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs, using either parallel-group or cross-over designs, that compared L-carnitine or its derivatives (acetyl-L-carnitine or propionyl-L-carnitine) with placebo or no treatment. Participants were cognitively healthy individuals of any age and gender, and trials of any dose or treatment duration were considered eligible. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were followed. Two independent reviewers selected trials, assessed their methodological quality, and extracted and analyzed data. However, only two RCTs met the inclusion criteria. One was a cross-over trial with 18 participants, while the other randomized 400 participants into four treatment groups, of which only the L-carnitine and placebo groups were relevant to this review. The exact number of participants in these two groups was not reported. All participants were young adults. Methodological details in both studies were poorly reported, and the risk of bias was deemed unclear. The two trials assessed different cognitive outcomes. From one trial, cognitive data for approximately 200 participants were extracted. This trial found no evidence that L-carnitine had any effect on reaction time, vigilance, immediate memory, or delayed recall after three days of treatment. The trial reported a small number of adverse effects, none of which were serious. The smaller cross-over trial also reported no cognitive effects of L-carnitine but did not provide data, nor did it report on adverse effects. The quality of the available evidence was considered very low for all reported outcomes. Due to the limited number of trials, the short duration of treatment, and inadequate reporting, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the efficacy or safety of L-carnitine for cognitive enhancement in healthy adults. Further well-designed, randomized, placebo-controlled trials with large sample sizes and longer follow-up periods are necessary to determine the potential role of L-carnitine in cognitive enhancement for this population.
